statement: You are given an undirected graph, made of a vertex count n (vertices numbered 0 to n − 1) and a list of edges, and a vertex start. Each vertex's neighbours are kept in the order their edges appear in the list.

Traverse the graph from start twice. Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue and visits vertices level by level: all neighbours of a vertex before any of their neighbours. Depth-first search (DFS) follows one neighbour as deep as it can go before backing up to try the next.
Return both visiting orders: bfsOrder for the breadth-first traversal and dfsOrder for the depth-first one. Both examples below use the same graph, to show how the two orders differ.

examples.explanation: BFS finishes the level {1, 2} before the level {3, 4, 5}, and reaches 6 last because it sits three edges from 0.
On the same graph DFS goes 0 → 1 → 3, backs up to 1, goes down 4 → 6, and only then returns to 0 to visit 2 and 5.
